utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the Defence counsel, to the Prosecution. We will now continue with the direct examination. The witness is not protected; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, no protective measures have been ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Zeljka Rajic, can we have Mrs. Rajic brought into the courtroom, please? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mrs. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Were you able to get some rest, Mrs. Rajic, relax a little bit after the difficult afternoon yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you feel all right? Can you continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you have any difficulty at all, whether psychological or physical, don't hesitate to ask for a break, and, of course, the Judges will order that the break take place so that you can rest. The Victims and Witnesses Unit is available to you if you need anything at all, all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence is not going to keep Mrs. Rajic much longer in direct examination, so we shall start immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Rajic, on the 27th of January, 1993, at around 9.00, you went to Zenica to see your parents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that? Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to Cajdras because they were following me. They wanted to have me killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You came to Cajdras on that very same day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on that very same day in the afternoon, around 4.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, after how many days did the funeral take place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Eight days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The videocassette that we saw yesterday, the dead bodies, did you see it at that time? If you did, where did you see it, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, not then, I didn't see it then. I saw it when I came to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see it in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: On television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On TV Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on TV Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the entire videocassette played on TV Busovaca, all these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the funeral, how did it take place? Where were the bodies brought? Where did the people assemble, those who came to attend the funeral of your husband and the others? Could you describe it a bit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: The funeral started in front of the house of the Croats, the Croatian Cultural Centre, towards Cajdras where the mass was held, and then straight to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Croats had assembled at the mass in Cajdras? How many Croats came to bid farewell to the persons killed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, about 3.000 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take buses to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, buses, cars, all kinds of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we please see the sequel to the videocassette. This is only the funeral in Busovaca, and there are no ugly scenes, so to speak. Could we please have the lights dimmed? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we are watching this tape, since there's no soundtrack, there's no text, tell me, these scenes that we are watching now, was this taped in Busovaca as people were assembling before going to the funeral?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Busovaca and in Zenica, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, how did this event resound among the Croats, and what did it mean in terms of the relationship between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it did resound. People could not simply realise this. They knew that they could no longer trust the Muslims. They had to flee from their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the first crime --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: The first crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- was this the first crime that occurred between the Muslims and the Croats in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first crime, yes, that event which took place in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as we're watching these scenes, are there any Croats living in Dusina today?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, no, their houses were burnt down and destroyed. Muslims live in our houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is somebody living in your house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your property, did you manage to salvage anything out of your movable property?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. Everything was destroyed, looted, up to the very last rag we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are still a refugee until the present day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that we can now finish viewing this videotape, and we have thus concluded our examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Mr. Cayley? Mr. Harmon, good afternoon. Mrs. Rajic, you're going to be asked some questions by the Office of the Prosecutor to supplement the direct examination. Don't be shocked by this. This is the procedural rule which is followed in this Tribunal. It has to be this way. Mr. Harmon, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions of Mrs. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, let me turn to my colleagues. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to know what number will be given or what will happen with the two exhibits that were presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We would like to have all these exhibits admitted into evidence, but the videotape could be a single exhibit, although we watched it twice or three times. So that would be D438 and D439, the newspapers, I mean. The tape is D438, and D439 are the newspapers that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe that Judge Riad wants to ask a few questions. Mr. Harmon, you have no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection to the admission of the exhibits, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Rajic. Please be assured that the entire Tribunal sympathises with your pain. I would only like to ask you, according to what you said, the attack on your village of Dusina was the first attack, the first crime?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there any incidents that provoked the attack, as far as you know? I'm sure that you were well-informed, a woman of your culture. Did anything happen that provoked the attack?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, no, nothing could have happened to lead to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there any declarations by politicians, any type of propaganda in the media, nothing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing of the sort. Had all of that not happened, we would have all stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen? Mrs. Rajic, I would like to join in fully of what Judge Riad said in respect of sympathy that the Tribunal has for what you have experienced and what happened afterwards and having to look at your husband's body. We hope that you can go back home and that you can resume if not a fully happy life, at least one that isn't too unhappy. That is what the Tribunal would like to say to you. We would like to thank you for having come to testify in this trial at the request of the Defence. At this time, the usher will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Hayman is standing up to represent the Defence for the next witness. I think I have a summary, do I not, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, you should have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is not, Mr. President. The next witness is Mr. Leyshon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, I don't seem to have ... do you have it, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was distributed this morning. It should arrive shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was just trying to ensure that Mr. Hayman doesn't have to repeat the summary which he's already given us. While you're looking for it, we'll ask Mr. Hayman to have the witness brought in. I know that I have it, so you don't have to do it now. We'll have the witness brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Do you hear me? Do you hear the Presiding Judge speaking to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please state your name, your given name, the date and place of your birth, your profession, and your current residence, and then please remain standing to take the oath. Proceed, please. The Judges are listening to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Chris Leyshon. I was born in London on the 14th of July, 1967. I currently work for an investment bank in London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the sake of the interpreters and for myself as well, perhaps you could spell your name. Oh, no, if the transcript is correct, there's no need to do so. Is the transcript correct? I don't have a summary in front of me. Is that correct? I won't have the witness repeat it if it is correct. Very well. Thank you. Please remain standing for a few more minutes to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, Mr. Leyshon. "Leyshon"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now you're going to answer the questions that you'll be asked, since you agreed to come to testify for the Defence in the trial of General Blaskic, who was Colonel Blaskic at the time of the facts, who stands accused of serious violations of humanitarian law. Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Leyshon. You are a former officer in the British army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe your career in the British army for the Court?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I joined the army directly from leaving university, and I went to Sandhurst where I trained for one year. I then joined my regiment, which was an infantry regiment, and served with them for five years. It was a short-service commission which basically meant that after a period of time I left the army, which I did do in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "short-service commission," did you agree to serve in the army as an officer for a period of time as part of that commission or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a contract basically to serve for three years, having graduated from Sandhurst, and I volunteered to extend for a further two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You look a bit back from the microphone. Perhaps you could pull your chair forward a bit and be comfortable. You said after you graduated from university, you went to Sandhurst for your officers training. From what university did you graduate in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Exeter University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you joined your regiment, can you tell the Court something about the tours of duty that you performed and the position or positions that you had in the regiment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. The university is Exeter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exeter, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They wrote it "Exody." It's a famous university. It should be written properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. We all know that under your Judge's robe is a great academic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would continue, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Having passed out of Sandhurst, I was posted to my regiment, the Cheshire Regiment, where I spent three months on an additional infantry training course in Warminster. I then rejoined my regiment, and three months later, we went to Northern Ireland for a six-month emergency tour of South Armagh. We then came back to England. The following year, we went out to Canada for three months live firing, and then we returned back to England once again where we were then posted to Germany to become an armoured infantry battalion where we spent two years. During that period of time, we were deployed for seven months to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your battalion was in Germany, did you have a particular position in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: When I joined the battalion in Germany, I was the intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you received certain specialised training before being given that position?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes. I had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. You don't need to elaborate, unless others feel it's necessary. I do not. From Germany, I take it your regiment went to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve with the regiment during the full regimental tour of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was from roughly October 1992 until May '93?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the British army?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: June '94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you left, were you offered a regular or permanent commission as an officer in the British army?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: During my short-service career, I had been offered an opportunity to take a regular commission, which I declined, and then when I was leaving the regiment in July '94, I was offered the position of intelligence officer for another two-year tour of Northern Ireland. However, I felt that I had done all I'd wanted to do in the army, and it was time to start a new career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you now live in London. Are you married and do you have a family?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm married and I have a son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than your tour of duty with the Cheshire Regiment, have you ever resided in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did you have in the Cheshire Regiment during its tour of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: My role was as the information officer, and I was there to collate information in order for the regiment to carry out its mission as effectively as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the head of what was known as the milinfocell?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you in charge of that cell?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that true for the entire tour of duty in the Cheshire Regiment in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes, until we handed over to the next regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could pause ever so briefly after my questions, it will perhaps help divide the question and answer when it is translated, and aid in comprehension of the material we're discussing. How many personnel in the regiment were part of the milinfocell?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: It varied slightly, but it was approximately seven personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, what was the mission or work of the milinfocell?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Our role was to collate information in order that we could carry out our mission effectively. Our mission was to support the UNHCR in the delivery of humanitarian aid, so our job primarily was to ensure where the routes were, how to deliver the aid, how to support the UNHCR, to identifying effectively where the frontline was so our units didn't cross the frontline, and to ensure the safety of those soldiers when escorting UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what source or sources of information did the milinfocell draw to gather information pertinent to these topics?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: There were a number of sources, both internal and external. Obviously there were our own soldiers on the ground who would be feeding us information all the time. We had approximately six liaison officers who were specifically there to ensure relationships with local commanders were good at all times, and they supplied us with a lot of information. The UNHCR also supplied us with quite a lot of information on routes and where local populations were and refugee movements, and of course, there were the local commanders, as well, the local Bosnian and Croatian commanders, who supplied us with a lot of information with respect to command structures, local commanders, frontlines, and information on Serbs, the Serbs, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally participate in the work of the milinfocell, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Our role was to collate the information on a daily basis, so obviously as various Cheshire call signs were going out on the ground and coming back, we would debrief them to get information from them. All the liaison officers would come speak to us at the end of the day to give us the information of who they had spoken to, if there were any issues or problems, and then we would collate all this information into a military information summary, and we would send it to Kiseljak, the headquarters for the U.N., and also to Split where the combritfor headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained you received certain information from call signs; can you explain what you mean by the term "call sign"?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes. A call sign is basically a unit on the ground, whether it's a Warrior vehicle, a Land Rover, it's basically any British army unit where it's a platoon, 30 men, or a liaison officer and his driver, out on the ground, coming back and then giving us information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the patrols or call signs, if one can equate the two, did they routinely travel out in the field with an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: We had a limited number of interpreters, approximately six or seven, and they were normally dedicated to the liaison officers and to the command structure, the commanding officer, the second in command. So your soldiers on the ground would not normally have an interpreter with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in the day were the milinfosums prepared?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, as soon as we got the information we would obviously collate that information. But normally it would be at the end of the day, usually from 6.00 onwards for a few hours, so they were normally completed by 9.00 or 10.00 every evening, and we would have all the information from that day's activity within that summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the milinfosum for a given day be transmitted to Kiseljak and Split on the same day or at some point on the following day?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: As long as the communications were available, which they were most of the time, it would always be sent that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days per week did you work in the milinfocell?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: It was a 7-day job, so the information was coming in every day. We didn't have days off so it was a fairly full-time job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally debrief liaison officers in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes, it would be either myself or my sort of main sergeant, Sergeant Connelly, who would have debriefed the liaison officers and the senior officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you review all the milinfosums before they went out on a routine basis?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes, unless I wasn't in camp or was out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one characterise the milinfocell as the centre of a wheel with spokes with information flowing towards the centre through various spokes?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, that's quite a good description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other routine or daily documents prepared by the regiment, such as a daily sitrep?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes, we were obviously focused on information, but there was obviously the operational responsibilities as well. So the operations officer would complete a similar report, but it would reflect operational activities, convoys escorted, various incidents, et cetera, et cetera, while we would be focusing more on the information where the frontline was, who the commanders were, what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive more information, in the course of an average day, than you could put in a milinfosum, or did all the information you receive go into the milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: All the information that we received, which we thought was of value, went into the summary each day. However, obviously there was some pieces of information which would be missed, because certain people would have seen things, but they wouldn't come and tell us what had happened, because there was such a large volume of movement, soldiers out on the ground. It's obviously impossible to get every piece of information, but we had a very good idea as to what was going on most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also, then, information gathered that wasn't deemed material or significant enough to put in the milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Sometimes a liaison officer would think there would be something which would be important, as far as they were concerned, but when you actually weigh it with the bigger picture of everything else going on, it was useful background information but it wasn't of real importance at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did most of the information that you deemed material and that was included in milinfosums, did it come from a particular source, and if so, what source?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, it was, as you already mentioned, it was human intelligence, human information from mostly the liaison officers. They were a prime source of material. And we did get a reasonable amount of information from local commanders, as well, and from other soldiers on the ground. But obviously, if you haven't got an interpreter with you, the amount of information you can actually gather is very limited, but obviously the soldiers on the ground can still see what's going on and report that. So it was from all sides, but the liaison officers were really one of the key areas of giving us information, because they were talking to the commanders, they had the interpreters with them, and they really had a very good feel for what was going on in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your work heading up the milinfocell for the British Battalion in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you come to a conclusion, or did you form a conclusion concerning what kind of army the HVO was, say compared to the British army?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, compared to the British army the HVO and the BiH were not professional armies. They were more like militias. They did not have very good command and control. Their soldiers weren't very well trained or equipped, and they were really, you know, very different. They were not professional armies, when you look at them compared to the British army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn whether or not the HVO soldiers were typically housed in barracks?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: There weren't that many barracks around. There were some barracks in Travnik, which I believe some Bosnian army brigades were located in, but the majority of locations where the HVO and BiH were, were normally requisitioned buildings, whether it be the local hotel where you would find the headquarters, or normally buildings such as schools which were no longer being used. These would be locations where soldiers would meet and congregate, but they weren't normally housed there, because there wasn't that much space to house all the soldiers. So they would probably normally, or a large proportion of them would probably go back to their homes when they would finish their duties, or if they weren't on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that have an effect on the type of army the HVO was, that soldiers lived at home in the villages, not in barracks?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it did. If you have soldiers who go home in their uniform and they have their weapons, and if they go out and have some drinks or go out drinking and have access to these weapons, what can start is simple arguments, or fracas can seriously escalate when people who are drunk have got access to weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that not happen in a professional army where soldiers live in barracks and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the British army, if a soldier is off duty he hands his weapon in, he goes out in civilian uniform. If they do get into trouble, which sometimes they do, they are not perfect, you know, it is not a serious incident. If you have a soldier who goes out and gets drunk and he has a weapon with him and he loses his temper, obviously the effect of that can be much worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, based on the information you came to possess as the head of the milinfosum, did you reach a conclusion as to the degree of command and control that existed within the HVO in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I would say the command and control was poor. These were not professional soldiers. It was untrained militias. A lot of soldiers weren't disciplined, they weren't well equipped. In order to have good command and control you've got to have good real-time communications. I didn't see much evidence of that. I didn't see a lot of radios on the ground. There was communication, so therefore, if you haven't got real-time communication, you don't have the opportunity to command and control your soldiers effectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see indications on the ground of this lack of command and control and if so, what types of indications did you see as reported to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: The main area of command and control which we saw in many different areas throughout our period of time was the lack of the ability to enforce cease-fire agreements. There were numerous times where we would get local Croatian and Bosnian army commanders together. We would broker a cease-fire, we would agree there would be a cessation of hostilities, and yet, days afterwards, there would still be fighting going on in the area which was theoretically under their command. This was because either they hadn't got the information there had been a cease-fire, or possibly they had, but they had decided to ignore it, because, you know, they were not professional soldiers. A lot of them were ill-disciplined, and a lot of them were sort of protecting their homes, as such. And a lot of things used to happen with a bit of sort of a tit for tat, someone would fire at someone and someone else would return fire and then things would escalate from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention briefly to the 16th of April, 1993, the day that a large scale conflict broke out in the Vitez and Lasva Valley areas. Did you conclude that the conflict that broke out on that day, on the 16th of April, that with respect to that conflict on the part of the HVO, the activity was organised? And if so, in what way was it organised?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I don't know if it was organised. The tensions had been rising for the last few days. There had been a number of kidnappings on both sides. Who actually started the fighting is unclear, but there was basically a very short period of time across the confrontation lines where any Croatian and Muslim village bordered, sat next to each other, there was some sort of fighting going on. So I don't know if it was organised and who initiated it, but it happened very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the information you received, did you conclude that the fact there was fighting in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, that it was likely known to the Operative Zone command of the HVO? And if so, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I should imagine the commander knew of the unit in that area. Whether or not he instructed them to attack Ahmici, I don't know. But I think there was a degree of organisation at a very low level, but whether or not it was a clear order is unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe the situation on the 16th of April, 1993 in the Lasva Valley as chaotic? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: It was very chaotic. There was a lot of fighting going on across the Lasva Valley, on both sides. And when things are chaotic, even a professional army would have problems finding out what was going on. And we didn't know what was going on all the time in all the places, but we had a rough idea what was going on most of the time. I don't think local commanders on both sides would have had a clear idea of what was going on, because their lines of communication were poor. So therefore, it was chaotic. I don't think they knew what was going on, and it was obvious when we had meetings with commanders that they didn't know exactly the dispositions of their soldiers or what they were doing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, may I have one moment just to pull an exhibit out with Mr. Harmon? Mr. President, if you will just bear with me one moment, I want to pull an exhibit up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You were surprised by the fact that the direct examination was so short. You see, we're not used to short direct examinations. I would like to take advantage of that in order to commend the Defence for the brevity and to have had the witness say what the Defence counsel wanted to have brought out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can begin while Mr. Harmon pulls this exhibit out. Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, good afternoon. My name is Greg Kehoe, I don't think we have had the pleasure of meeting, sir. I know you know Major Cayley, over to my right. You had an opportunity to meet him before. And my other colleague with me is Mr. Hayman. Welcome. Excuse me, Mr. Hayman -- Mr. Harmon. It was a Freudian slip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You were worrying me. I thought that the witness knew everybody in the Prosecution's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I worry myself sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, we're not going to ask the witness to supplement the staff of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, you say that you were working in the milinfocell and that you prepared these milinfosums, I take it, on a daily basis, getting information from other locales; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, isn't it true that you spent virtually all of your time at the Vitez school, or the Bila school during the course of your tour?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I did have to spend a lot of time obviously working, but a lot of my responsibilities could be completed in the evening, and I spent a lot of time going out with liaison officers. I went up to Tuzla. I went to Sarajevo, and I spent a lot of time in Travnik and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's clear, Mr. Leyshon, that you didn't spend, on a daily basis, out on the ground dealing with commanders --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What happened? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think they were telling us to slow down, Judge. Both Mr. Leyshon and I speak the same language, so it's a little difficult on interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Leyshon, let's go back to some of the statements that you made during the course of your direct examination in questions by the Defence and you stated that, compared to the British army, the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not professional armies like the British army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Before the witness answers, I want things to be clear. You cannot use up more time than was used for the direct examination. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Reluctantly, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to tell you that right now. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree, Judge, but reluctantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, Judge, just for the record, so I know how to pace myself, what do I have, about 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The direct was 25 minutes and Mr. Kehoe has 20 minutes left, if a 25-minute restriction is going to be placed on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the direct examination lasted for 20 or 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was 23 minutes and a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, 23 minutes. You began 3 minutes ago, therefore you have until the break, that is until ten to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this particular witness has come in with some very broad, sweeping claims concerning command and control. And while the direct examination may have only been 20 to 25 minutes, without a cross examination that goes into the documents and exploring the depths of Mr. Leyshon's knowledge, I submit to Your Honours and you, Mr. President, that Your Honours are not going to get a full appreciation of what this witness does and does not know, with all due respect, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Twenty minutes, we have agreed. I understand your problem. The direct examination was short and only dealt with a specific number of points, so limit yourself to those points. We're wasting time. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, you said that compared to the British army that the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not the professional army that the British army was; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me that the British army has, well, a pretty distinguished military career going back hundreds and hundreds of years, including the Cheshire Regiment, which I believe goes back to sometime in the 17th Century; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the former Yugoslavia itself was only in existence from approximately 1945; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I believe you're correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to let the interpreters catch up. Mr. Leyshon, what was the structure of the armed forces in the former Yugoslavia, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1945 until their decline and fall in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, I don't know a huge amount about the JNA, apart from the fact they were trained and equipped with the Russian-style tactics. The majority of the JNA were of Serb decent, and when the country broke up the majority of equipment and experience ended up in Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is, what was the actual internal structure of the JNA? How did it operate? Was it based on a structure such as the British army? Was it based on a different structure that dealt with Territorial Defence units? How was it based, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, I don't know a huge amount about the JNA, but you can quite easily judge whether an army is professional or not by looking at its operations, the way it behaves, if soldiers are disciplined. And those are the qualities which I'm judging the HVO and the Bosnian army on in seven months experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did HVO soldiers follow orders?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I don't know. Some did, some didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me an example of one where you know, based on your own personal experience, where an HVO soldier didn't follow an order.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I can show orders, I can't prove that, because obviously I didn't have access to the HVO command structure. But I can show examples of where HVO soldiers were undisciplined and obviously could not have been following orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Defence object 267, 268 and 269, if we could do that, Mr. Usher. And if I could ask the usher to run, that would be helpful. Have you seen these orders before you came here, Mr. Leyshon?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman showed them to me this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he show you all of the orders that were executed by then Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I've only looked at a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which ones did you look at?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I've seen this one before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the next one.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I haven't read all this, but I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman showed you that?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them when you were on the ground in Bosnia, in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No, we wouldn't have seen any orders. These would have been secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you see any written orders at all that General Blaskic gave to his troops when they were on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: The only output I saw would have been at brokered peace agreements where both Mr. Blaskic and his counter party from the Bosnian army agreed to a cease-fire and the rules of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's go with that. Would that be the cease-fire orders that were executed on the 13th of February of 1993? Did you see those?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: With respect to which area were they?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Central Bosnia. You were the intelligence officer at the time collating information.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Part of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was signed in Kakanj and dealt with the Busovaca and Vitez area; did you see those cease-fire orders?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Busovaca, I believe there was -- I've got some milinfosums here, actually, so I can probably tell you exactly. What date did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 13th of February, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, I've got notes here saying preliminary meetings on the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Leyshon, would you accept the fact that Defence has admitted evidence of cease-fire agreements dated the 13th of February, 1993, signed by the accused, as well as General Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sure you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they stop fighting?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: In Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vitez, after the 13th of February, 1993, did they stop fighting?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: As far as I can relate, probably not everywhere, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the troops stop the war? Barring for sporadic fire, sir, did the troops stop fighting with one another, army against army?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: In Busovaca, September 13 onwards?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: February.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: February, sorry. I can't actually accurately answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cease-fire worked, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No, I just said I can't accurately -- we had a number of cease-fires. We had a similar agreement in Gornji Vakuf at the same time; that cease-fire failed. And looking at my notes now, I'm sure I could probably pull out numerous examples of fighting in the Busovaca area, whether that be sporadic arms fire or actual artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that another indication of a lack of command and control and the difficulty of command and control is the fact that without proper communications the commanding officer doesn't know where his troops are and he can't communicate with them properly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: If you haven't got real-time communications, you cannot command subunits on the ground if they are engaged in any sort of action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Leyshon, let me show you Prosecution Exhibit 456/45, as well as Defence Exhibit 305 and Defence Exhibit 306. If we could show Mr. Leyshon first 356/45 to be followed by Defence Exhibits 305 and 306, that would be helpful. Do you see that sir? Did Mr. Hayman show you that Exhibit? I'm talking about Prosecution Exhibit 456/45.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, again, I've seen this but I haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at it, and please note the time, and please note the time at which combat activities were to begin, and I refer you to paragraph 10 on page 2?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Who is this sent to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at it, sir. Who is it sent to? It's sent to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak. And, at that time, Mr. Leyshon, the road between Kiseljak and Busovaca was cut in half with the BiH army controlling between Kacuni and Bilalovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Not on the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I think that we will all stipulate on the 17th of April, that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was firmly ensconced, that's one thing that the Defence and the Prosecution will clearly agree on, firmly ensconced in the Kacuni area. Now, you take a look at that order, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at the reply back, Exhibit 305 and 306, and I will tell you that there's evidence been submitted to this Tribunal that the combat activities in Kiseljak municipality did, in fact, take place at 0530 on the morning of the 18th of April. Take a look at the responding orders, 305 and 306. Now, 305 is a report back at 1000 hours from the officer on duty from the Ban Jelacic Brigade discussing the execution of that order and combat activities, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes. He's issued some orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's issued some orders, and the orders were followed, and this is a reply back coming from the Ban Jelacic Brigade at 1000 hours the following morning concerning the update on those activities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, this is what the piece of paper in front of me is saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a Defence Exhibit, sir. Trust me. It's Defence Exhibit 305.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm not saying that this is not inaccurate --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If this is accurate, sir, would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can the witness finish his answer, Your Honour? Mr. Kehoe is interrupting the witness.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: What I'm saying is I'm sure this is a correct piece of documentation. What I'm saying is it actually what actually happened on the ground? Is that a true reflection of what happened on the ground?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if this document is a true reflection of what happened on the ground, would you agree with me, Mr. Leyshon, that communications were pretty good?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: How was this documentation sent?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This has been submitted by the Defence as a document, submitted by a Defence witness in this Tribunal, Mr. Leyshon.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah. But, again, we're talking about reports which are being sent. We've got a report here which is sent on the 17th of April at 2345 hours, and we have another report which is sent the next day at 1000 hours. That's not real-time reporting. Yes, some orders have been issued, I agree, and there are responses being sent back. When did he receive this report back? This is not real-time communication. That is not a normal communication you would associate with a professional body of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, an order is given out on the evening of the 17th of April at 2345 to execute combat operations the next morning at 0530 on the morning of the 18th. The evidence before this Tribunal is that combat activities did commence at 0530 on the morning of the 18th of April. The evidence is also based on Defence witnesses. Defence Exhibit 305 is the first report received back from the Ban Jelacic Brigade concerning those activities. Given those facts, Mr. Leyshon, wouldn't you agree that the communications that the HVO possessed were pretty good?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another thing you said is that, based on communications and some difficulties, if the commanding officer doesn't know where his troops are, it's awfully difficult to stay in control of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah. You've got to have real-time communications to know exactly what your subunits are doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because where the attacks take place, you want to know where offensive and defensive positions are, et cetera; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's right. If you don't know what your subunits are doing, if they are achieving a task or not, you have to make command decisions from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me show you Prosecution Exhibit 456/38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see you looking at that clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge, like the other Judges, is not petty. We're trying to maintain an equitable balance here. You know, as regards the communications, go to the end of the questions that you want to ask. You've started a demonstration of something. Go to the end. That's fine. Thank you. Ask your questions calmly. If necessary, we will take a few more minutes. Give the witness time to look at the documents and answer as he wants to, while I give the French version of this to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. It should have been 32, I apologise, 456/32, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn you to these versions. This is a document that is executed by Colonel Blaskic on the 7th of May, 1993, and I would turn you to the page that says "Thrusts of the attack," and I think that is one, two, three, four, five, six pages in. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Just getting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that particular segment notes the thrusts of the attack and gives any number of locations where the attacks were taking place; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: These are attacks during what period of time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular document deals with the attacks that begin on the 16th and go through until this report on the 17th -- on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that knowing what locations are being attacked, either offensively or defensively, indicates that a commander knows exactly what's going on in the field?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, looking at this piece of paper here in front of me, is this a true reflection of what actually happened on the ground, it's very difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you present in the meeting with Colonel Watters, General Halilovic, Colonel Hadzihasanovic, General Petkovic, and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I wasn't present at the whole meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if Colonel Watters, now the commander of the Cheshire Regiment, indicated that Blaskic was fully aware of the positions of all of his troops, as well as the troops of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that indicate to you that General Blaskic knew what was happening, knew how to communicate with these people, and essentially knew what was going on?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: He might know where his soldiers are positioned at a certain point in time. Whether or not he has a real-time idea of where his soldiers are all the time, I would say that that would be less likely. Whether or not he knows if those soldiers are carrying out his orders, if those soldiers are doing exactly what he is saying, again, I would say it would be unlikely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Leyshon, who do you think would have a better idea of how command and control functioned within the HVO? Would you have a better idea or would Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic would have a better knowledge of the HVO command and control structure, but I could still make an educated military opinion on what I saw on the ground during seven months, and that opinion is that there was not a good degree of command and control with their soldiers on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: Who would have a better idea, you or Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: A better idea of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of command and control, whether or not command and control functioned properly?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, I would have better real-time communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would know better than Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I would have a more -- I may have had a better idea during the time that all the fighting was going on in the Lasva Valley, of where the fighting was going on, because I had lots of call signs out on the ground all reporting into the Cheshire ops room telling us where the fighting was, who was engaged in what. All these call signs all had radios, and all the reporting was real-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, you never saw an order written by Colonel Blaskic at the time, you never saw any of the deployment orders, you don't know what oral orders he was giving to the troops, and you're telling this Court, based on everything that you don't know, that you had a better idea of whether command and control was functioning properly than Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered. That's an objection. To the witness, you wait for the Court to respond, please. My objection is asked and answered, the same question now three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think you've asked that question several times, Mr. Kehoe. That's true. Do you know who was the most likely to understand the value of the communication and the quality of the information, either the witness or the accused, in terms of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Leyshon, turn to the page on conclusions. Now, the conclusion written by Colonel Blaskic to the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is the following: "Command and control function properly and all missions proceed in a planned fashion according to orders, with detailed knowledge of the situation, full coordination and control." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen that before you came in here today?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, I have seen part of these documents before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman showed you that document as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You discussed that document with him?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: He showed me some parts of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Prosecutor's Exhibit 380, if we could. Now, this document 380 is an article from an interview of the defendant Danas. Did you see this article before?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman showed you that article as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I saw it this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we can move through it quickly. In this article again, in the first paragraph, the bottom line, the last two sentences, Blaskic says, "All operative groups are under my command, and the chain of leadership and command function absolutely without interruption." Now, that particular statement is consistent with the statement that he gave to his own commanders in Mostar, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Who did he give this statement to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To a newspaper article, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Right. Well, would you expect a military commander to say anything else to a newspaper? If he was to say, "I hadn't --" if we hadn't operated effectively, he would actually be saying, "I'm not a good commander."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, is what he said in the newspaper article consistent with what he told his commanders on the 7th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, yeah, it's a very similar paragraph but is it consistent with what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what he told to the people in charge, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: The same answer, I'm afraid. You are going to tell your superior officer that you're doing a good job. It's human nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir. So if command and control didn't work in a particular platoon that you were under operation, you wouldn't tell the regimental commander that things weren't working? You would lie to him? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that if a senior officer, like Colonel Blaskic, was reporting upwards, it's more likely that he's going to report that he's doing a good job, he's an effective commander, and that he's carried out his mission correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Leyshon, that a commanding officer in the British army would tell his superior and lie to his superior about what was taking place? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that it is likely that a commander will think he's doing a good job, and he will give the information upwards that he has good command and control of his unit. That might not necessarily be a true reflection of the facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your conclusion is that Blaskic believed that command and control worked properly?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: He may have thought that by the standards of his units, which were unprofessional, ill-disciplined units, he had a level of command of control which is all that he could expect from those units. It was what he had. He was making the best of a poor situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The system that you are comparing it to is that of the British army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's right, a professional army with command and control. And you can only have command and control if you've got real-time communications, which I don't believe he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, Mr. Leyshon, that Blaskic believed that he had command and control over his troops, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: He had the level of command and control, I should imagine, you could ever hope for with the resources available to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if something is wrong, generally, a commanding officer will ask for help, won't he?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I don't know. It varies from army to army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the British army, they would ask for help, wouldn't they, Mr. Leyshon?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: They would but that's a professional army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, let me show you Prosecution Exhibit 512, one of your milinfosums, and you can take a look at it while we're waiting. It's February 1, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is the last exhibit that you're going to show the witness, the last question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have one question after this particular exhibit, which will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, do you see the milinfosum of 1 February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a military information summary that sets out a chain of command, does it not? I turn to the third page of that milinfosum; do you see that? Did you write that or assist in the writing of it or review it or approve it or anything?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't remember who wrote it, but I probably would have seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the HVO had a recognisable structure with a hierarchy and a chain of command that you set forth in that document; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the structure and chain of command that Blaskic, himself, says worked; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, I would disagree that it was an efficient chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I mean, it is written on paper, correct, but how effective that chain of command was is questionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I beg to ask for a little bit more time. I have a little bit more to ask in this rather sweeping testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues because this is a question of principle here. Mr. Kehoe, the Judges give you until 4.15 to complete your cross-examination. I apologise to the interpreters. We will work until a quarter after, and these few extra moments will not be counted as Defence time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Leyshon, when you were analysing the command and control within the HVO, did you analyse the background of HVO officers?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I don't know. That wasn't our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't your job when you were making a decision about the command and control of HVO officers?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, our job wasn't to analyse HVO officers. Our job was to know who the commanders were, so when there were problems on the ground, we knew which commanders to talk to to try and broker agreements, cease-fire agreements, and ensure that we could complete our mission. Our mission, at the end of the day, was to ensure that humanitarian aid got delivered, not to collect intelligence on local commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would it be important for your consideration, Mr. Leyshon, to know the military background of HVO officers when you're making your decision on command and control?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: It would be a factor, definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I was judging what I saw on the ground over a long period of time. It wasn't a snap judgment. It was a judgment made -- I saw lots of incidents of ill-disciplined soldiers on all sides and poor command and control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, did you see HVO training manuals?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see HVO training going on?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was HVO training going on?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see it, then I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at 456/32 and go back to that page we talked about in conclusions. Go back to that conclusions page.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 2 in the conclusions and read it for us out loud.

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: "Training and education - younger troops (especially in Busovaca 38 killed and 108 wounded so far) are undergoing special training according to the submitted training plan."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would General Blaskic know more about training of HVO troops or you?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, he would know more about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from that, he concludes that training is taking place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No. He's saying that they are undergoing special training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't that mean that they are undergoing training, Mr. Leyshon?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, it means that he's written on a piece of paper to his headquarter that they are undergoing training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, wait a second, Mr. Leyshon. He is writing a report to his commanders in Mostar telling them that younger troops are undergoing special training according to the submitted training plan. Does the document say that?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's what the document says, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you raising the question with this Court that, while Blaskic writes that on a piece of paper, he may not be telling his commanders the truth?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the command structure below him may have been that this training might not have happened. Some of it might have happened; some of it might not have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis do you make that statement to these Judges? What factual basis do you have for that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, I don't see how a huge amount of training could have gone on, looking at the quality or discipline of these soldiers. They were not professional soldiers, and they didn't appear to be very well-trained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, what facts do you have to support your allegation that no training was taking place and that this statement is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I can only base it on the fact that I never saw any training, and I never had any reports of any training going on from any of the soldiers within our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know one way or the other, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, we had a lot of people out on the ground for seven months, and not once did we see any existence of any training going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, did you receive reliable information that the HVO were burning houses of Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Yeah, there were examples of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you turn your attention to Gornji Vakuf on the 6th of February. Take a look at your milinfosums on the 6th of February. In the paragraph under Gornji Vakuf, did you write, "Last night, it was reported that HVO Commander Zrinko Topcic issued an ultimatum to the BiH forces to surrender their weapons to the HVO. If they refused, he would burn the town to the ground."

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I can't remember if I wrote it. It would have been reported to us from our milinfosum in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would have been B Company under the command of Major Rule; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of this statement?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also receive information concerning trench digging by the HVO of Bosnian Muslim civilians, and let me cut through this, and why don't you page up just one page and stay with the 6th of February in the Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope, Mr. President. Counsel can go on regarding command and control, whatever, as the Court is going to permit him, but beyond the scope, I think, poses a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that's outside the scope of the direct examination. Once again, I take the liberty of saying to you that the witness was called by the Defence to testify about specific points. You can have him tell about the seven months of war, that's another option, but I believe that the Trial Chamber has given you additional time. Do you have one further question to ask, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during your direct examination that the attack that took place on Ahmici was an organised attack; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: There was a degree of organisation, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Leyshon, that attack took place in Ahmici, Santici, Pirici, Donja Veceriska, and Stari Vitez all at the same time, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: There was a lot of fighting going on across the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All those attacks took place on the morning of the 16th; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: I don't believe that there was the same level of activity in those other villages as there was in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you concluded at the time that the HVO was the attacking force; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRIS LEYSHON
utterances.text: Well, yeah, that's quite an easy assessment to make when it's a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you noted in your conversation with Dai Morriss and with Mr. Cayley that it was unlikely that, given the number of soldiers involved, the HVO command did not have knowledge of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I inquire and interrupt? Your Honour, if counsel is referring to a witness statement, we were never given a witness statement for this witness, although he was listed as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There's no signed witness statement. There is no signed witness statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that to be false because I got it from the witness, and he signed it and faxed it to the Office of the Prosecutor, and they never gave it to the Defence. It's been filed with this Court and Your Honours have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't have it. I have an unsigned witness statement, unsigned, never executed, never reviewed by this witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what did you say? You were relying on what document, on the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. There were notes taken by Mr. Morriss that were put together in his interview that Mr. Cayley participated in. They drafted this up. This was never reviewed by this witness, nor was it signed in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor at all, ever. It was never compiled for this particular person to sign, and the reason for that was that was relatively information-free. Now, if counsel has a signed copy, that is news to the Prosecutor, Mr. President, big news.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's already been filed with the Court. It speaks for itself. Signed, faxed, in their possession. He was put on the Prosecutor's witness list. They had a signed statement. They didn't give it to us, and now the Court knows why, having heard the testimony of this witness.
